title: Getting Things Done
author: David Allen
description: David Allen's productivity method for capturing every task and commitment in a trusted external system, then deciding the next physical action for each. It explains how to organise projects, lists and weekly reviews so the mind is free to focus. Useful for students and professionals juggling many responsibilities.

title: The Road Less Traveled
author: M. Scott Peck
description: A psychiatrist reflects on discipline, love, growth and responsibility, arguing that accepting life's difficulties is the starting point for maturity. Drawing on cases from his practice, Peck connects psychological health with personal and spiritual development. Suited to readers interested in reflective, values-based self-improvement.

title: Ikigai
author: Héctor García
description: An introduction to the Japanese idea of ikigai, a sense of purpose that gives each day meaning. The authors draw on interviews with long-lived residents of Okinawa to discuss routines, diet, community and work. A short, gentle read for anyone thinking about balance and purpose.

title: The Magic of Thinking Big
author: David J. Schwartz
description: A classic on how beliefs and self-image shape what people attempt and achieve. Schwartz offers practical techniques for building confidence, overcoming excuses and setting ambitious goals. Written for readers starting a career or looking to raise their own expectations.

title: Make Your Bed
author: William H. McRaven
description: A retired US Navy admiral expands a well-known commencement speech into ten lessons drawn from SEAL training and military service. Each chapter links a small habit or experience to resilience, teamwork and perseverance. Brief and anecdotal, aimed at general readers and graduates.

title: Tiny Habits
author: BJ Fogg
description: A Stanford behaviour researcher presents a method for building habits by starting with very small actions tied to existing routines. The book explains his model of motivation, ability and prompts, with worked examples and exercises. Practical for anyone who has struggled to make new habits last.

title: Four Thousand Weeks
author: Oliver Burkeman
description: Starting from the fact that an average lifetime is about four thousand weeks, Burkeman questions conventional productivity advice. He argues for accepting limits, choosing priorities deliberately and tolerating unfinished tasks. A thoughtful read for people who feel overwhelmed by busyness.

title: Boundaries
author: Henry Cloud
description: Two clinical psychologists explain how to set healthy limits in relationships with family, friends, partners and colleagues. They describe common boundary problems and offer guidance on saying no and taking responsibility for one's own choices. Written from a Christian perspective.

title: Psycho-Cybernetics
author: Maxwell Maltz
description: A plastic surgeon's account of how self-image influences behaviour and how it can be changed through visualisation and mental rehearsal. Maltz combines observations from his patients with exercises for goal setting and confidence. A foundational text for many later self-help programmes.

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up
author: Marie Kondo
description: Marie Kondo describes her method of decluttering by category and keeping only items that genuinely matter to the owner. The book covers how to sort clothes, books, papers and keepsakes, and how to store what remains. Helpful for readers who want an orderly living or study space.

title: The Daily Stoic
author: Ryan Holiday
description: A year of daily readings, each pairing a short passage from Stoic philosophers such as Marcus Aurelius, Seneca and Epictetus with a brief commentary. Monthly themes cover clarity, emotions, action and acceptance. Designed as a daily companion for reflection.

title: Fluent Python
author: Luciano Ramalho
description: An in-depth guide to writing idiomatic Python by understanding the language's data model, data structures, functions, objects and concurrency features. Each chapter explains why Python behaves as it does, with many runnable examples. Best for programmers who already know basic Python and want to master it.

title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python
author: Al Sweigart
description: A beginner-friendly introduction to Python focused on practical scripts for everyday tasks. Readers learn the basics of the language, then use it to work with files, spreadsheets, PDFs, web pages, email and the keyboard and mouse. No prior programming experience is assumed.

title: Working Effectively with Legacy Code
author: Michael Feathers
description: A practical handbook for changing large existing codebases that lack tests. Feathers presents techniques for breaking dependencies, getting code under test and making safe changes step by step. Valuable for developers maintaining real-world software in Java, C++, C and similar languages.

title: Head First Java
author: Kathy Sierra
description: A visually rich introduction to Java and object-oriented programming that uses puzzles, diagrams and conversational explanations. It covers classes, inheritance, polymorphism, exceptions, collections and basic GUI and networking topics. Aimed at beginners and students taking a first Java course.

title: The Rust Programming Language
author: Steve Klabnik
description: The official introductory book on Rust, written by members of the Rust team. It teaches ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, error handling, traits and concurrency through explanations and small projects. Suitable for programmers with experience in another language who want to learn Rust.

title: Test Driven Development: By Example
author: Kent Beck
description: Kent Beck demonstrates test-driven development by building code through short cycles of writing a failing test, making it pass and refactoring. Worked examples show the rhythm of the practice, followed by patterns for applying it. A core reference for developers learning TDD.

title: Effective C++
author: Scott Meyers
description: A collection of specific guidelines for writing better C++, each explained with examples and reasoning. Topics include resource management, constructors and destructors, inheritance, templates and designing clear interfaces. Intended for programmers who already know C++ basics.

title: Modern Operating Systems
author: Andrew S. Tanenbaum
description: A widely used textbook on how operating systems work, covering processes and threads, memory management, file systems, input/output, deadlocks, virtualisation and security. Case studies of Linux, Android and Windows connect the theory to real systems. Intended for undergraduate operating systems courses.

title: Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software
author: Charles Petzold
description: Petzold builds up an explanation of how computers work, starting from simple codes like Morse and Braille and moving through relays, logic gates, binary arithmetic, memory and processors. It requires no technical background. A good companion for students beginning computer science or electronics.

title: Concrete Mathematics
author: Ronald L. Graham
description: A mathematics textbook covering the techniques most useful for analysing algorithms, including sums, recurrences, integer functions, binomial coefficients, generating functions and asymptotics. It grew out of a Stanford course and includes many exercises with answers. Suited to computer science students with a solid maths foundation.

title: Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications
author: Kenneth H. Rosen
description: A comprehensive introduction to discrete mathematics for computing, covering logic, proofs, sets, functions, counting, probability, relations, graphs, trees and Boolean algebra. Each topic is linked to applications in computer science, with extensive exercises. A standard text for first-year discrete maths courses.

title: Gödel, Escher, Bach
author: Douglas R. Hofstadter
description: Hofstadter explores how meaning and self-awareness might arise from formal systems, weaving together Gödel's incompleteness theorem, Escher's art and Bach's music. Dialogues between characters alternate with chapters on logic, computation and cognition. A long, playful read for those curious about minds, mathematics and AI.

title: Algorithm Design
author: Jon Kleinberg
description: A textbook that teaches how to design algorithms by working from real problems to solutions. It covers greedy methods, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, network flow, NP-completeness, approximation and randomised algorithms. Aimed at upper-level undergraduate and graduate algorithms courses.

title: Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation
author: John E. Hopcroft
description: A classic textbook on the theory of computation, covering finite automata, regular expressions, context-free grammars, pushdown automata, Turing machines, decidability and complexity. Proofs are presented with examples and exercises. Used in theory of computation and compiler foundation courses.

title: Engineering a Compiler
author: Keith D. Cooper
description: A textbook on building modern compilers, from scanning and parsing through intermediate representations, optimisation, instruction selection, register allocation and scheduling. It emphasises practical engineering trade-offs alongside the underlying theory. Suitable for undergraduate and graduate compiler courses.

title: Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis in C++
author: Mark Allen Weiss
description: A textbook that teaches core data structures, such as lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, heaps and graphs, alongside the analysis of algorithms that use them. Examples are written in C++, and the book covers sorting and algorithm design techniques. Designed for second-year data structures courses.

title: Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach
author: Sanjeev Arora
description: A graduate-level textbook on computational complexity theory, covering P and NP, space complexity, the polynomial hierarchy, randomised computation, interactive proofs, circuit lower bounds and PCP theorems. It combines classical results with more recent developments. Intended for advanced students and researchers in theoretical computer science.

title: The Annotated Turing
author: Charles Petzold
description: Petzold guides readers line by line through Alan Turing's 1936 paper that introduced the Turing machine. He supplies the mathematical and historical background needed to follow it, along with notes on Turing's life. Useful for students who want to understand the foundations of computation from the original source.

title: Algorithms to Live By
author: Brian Christian
description: The authors show how ideas from computer science, such as optimal stopping, sorting, caching, scheduling and game theory, can inform everyday decisions. Each chapter explains an algorithmic idea in plain language and applies it to human situations. An accessible read for general audiences and students.

title: Introduction to Computing Systems
author: Yale N. Patt
description: A bottom-up introduction to computing that starts with bits and transistors and progresses through logic circuits, a simple computer architecture, machine and assembly language, and finally C programming. It helps students see how high-level code maps to hardware. Commonly used in first computer engineering courses.

title: Digital Design and Computer Architecture
author: David Money Harris
description: A textbook that moves from digital logic and hardware description languages to the design of a working processor. It covers combinational and sequential circuits, assembly language, microarchitecture and memory systems. Aimed at students in introductory computer architecture and digital design courses.

title: The Little Book That Still Beats the Market
author: Joel Greenblatt
description: A hedge fund manager explains a simple, rules-based approach to value investing, often called the magic formula, that ranks companies by earnings yield and return on capital. He uses everyday examples to show why buying good businesses at bargain prices works over time. Written for beginners to stock investing.

title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
author: Ramit Sethi
description: A six-week programme for young adults on managing money, covering credit cards, bank accounts, automated saving, conscious spending and low-cost investing. Sethi focuses on systems that run with little effort. Aimed at students and early-career earners starting to take control of their finances.

title: Your Money or Your Life
author: Vicki Robin
description: This book asks readers to measure money in terms of the life energy spent earning it. It sets out a step-by-step programme for tracking income and spending, reducing waste and working towards financial independence. Useful for anyone rethinking the relationship between work, money and values.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham
description: The foundational text of value investing, explaining how to analyse bonds and stocks using financial statements and a margin of safety. Later editions include commentary from modern investors relating the ideas to current markets. A demanding reference for serious students of finance.

title: Irrational Exuberance
author: Robert J. Shiller
description: A Nobel-winning economist examines speculative bubbles in stock, bond and housing markets. Shiller combines historical data with psychological and cultural factors to explain why prices can drift far from fundamentals. Relevant to students of economics, finance and market behaviour.

title: The Most Important Thing
author: Howard Marks
description: Investor Howard Marks sets out the principles behind his approach, including second-level thinking, understanding risk, market cycles and patience. Each chapter focuses on one idea, drawn from his client memos. Aimed at readers who want to think more carefully about investing.

title: The Big Short
author: Michael Lewis
description: Lewis tells the story of a few investors who foresaw the collapse of the US housing market and bet against subprime mortgage bonds before the 2008 financial crisis. The book explains the financial products involved through the people who studied them. An accessible account of how the crisis unfolded.

title: Flash Boys
author: Michael Lewis
description: An account of high-frequency trading in US stock markets and a group of traders who set out to expose how speed advantages affected ordinary investors. Lewis explains market structure, exchanges and order routing in plain language. Of interest to readers curious about modern financial markets and technology.

title: Liar's Poker
author: Michael Lewis
description: Michael Lewis recounts his years as a bond salesman at Salomon Brothers in the 1980s. The memoir describes trading floor culture, the rise of mortgage bonds and the excesses of Wall Street at the time. A readable introduction to how investment banks operated.

title: When Genius Failed
author: Roger Lowenstein
description: The story of Long-Term Capital Management, a hedge fund run by star traders and Nobel laureates that collapsed in 1998 and required a rescue organised by the Federal Reserve. Lowenstein explains the fund's strategies, leverage and the risks they overlooked. A case study in financial risk for students and general readers.

title: Die with Zero
author: Bill Perkins
description: Perkins argues that people often save too much for too long and miss experiences that matter most at particular ages. He offers ways to plan spending, giving and work so that money supports a fulfilling life. A thought-provoking read on personal finance and life planning.

title: Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
author: John C. Hull
description: A standard textbook on derivative securities, covering futures, forwards, swaps, options, pricing models such as Black-Scholes, and risk management. It balances theory with market practice and numerical methods. Widely used in finance degree programmes and by practitioners.

title: The Ascent of Money
author: Niall Ferguson
description: A historian traces the development of money, credit, banking, bonds, stocks, insurance and real estate from ancient times to the modern global economy. Ferguson links financial innovations to major historical events. A broad, accessible history for general readers and students.

title: Money: Master the Game
author: Tony Robbins
description: Tony Robbins condenses interviews with prominent investors into a seven-step plan for personal financial freedom. Topics include saving, fees, asset allocation, retirement income and avoiding common mistakes. Written for general readers who want a broad overview of personal investing.

title: Built to Last
author: Jim Collins
description: A study of companies that remained leaders in their industries over many decades, compared with similar firms that fell behind. The authors identify shared traits such as a core ideology, bold goals and a culture that preserves values while encouraging progress. Aimed at managers and business students.

title: Start with Why
author: Simon Sinek
description: Sinek argues that inspiring leaders and organisations communicate their purpose, their why, before explaining what they do and how. He illustrates the idea with examples from companies and public figures. A popular read on leadership, communication and motivation.

title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
author: Patrick Lencioni
description: A fictional story of a new chief executive working to rebuild a struggling leadership team, followed by a practical model. Lencioni identifies five problems, from absence of trust to inattention to results, and how to address them. Widely used in team-building and management training.

title: Crossing the Chasm
author: Geoffrey A. Moore
description: Moore explains why many technology products struggle to move from early adopters to mainstream customers. He describes the technology adoption life cycle and offers a strategy for targeting a niche market to cross the gap. A standard read for marketers and technology entrepreneurs.

title: Competitive Strategy
author: Michael E. Porter
description: Porter's classic framework for analysing industries and competitors, including the five forces that shape competition and the generic strategies firms can adopt. It provides tools for understanding industry structure and positioning. A core text in business strategy courses.

title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy
author: Richard P. Rumelt
description: Rumelt explains what makes a strategy effective: a clear diagnosis, a guiding policy and coherent actions. He contrasts this with common failures such as vague goals and fluff, using examples from business and history. Useful for managers, students and anyone responsible for planning.

title: Radical Candor
author: Kim Scott
description: A former technology executive presents a framework for managers based on caring personally while challenging directly. Scott gives practical advice on giving and receiving feedback, building relationships and guiding teams. Helpful for new and experienced managers.

title: High Output Management
author: Andrew S. Grove
description: Andy Grove, former chief executive of Intel, explains management as a production process. He covers meetings, decision-making, planning, performance reviews and training, with an emphasis on a manager's output. A classic guide for new managers, especially in technology.

title: Who Says Elephants Can't Dance?
author: Louis V. Gerstner
description: Louis Gerstner recounts how he led IBM's turnaround in the 1990s, when the company was close to collapse. He describes decisions on strategy, culture and keeping the company together. A first-hand case study in large-scale corporate change.

title: The Everything Store
author: Brad Stone
description: A journalist's account of the founding and growth of Amazon and the management style of Jeff Bezos. Based on interviews with current and former employees, it follows the company from an online bookstore to a global retailer and cloud provider. Of interest to business and technology readers.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip Heath
description: The Heath brothers examine why some ideas are remembered and others forgotten. They propose six principles, including simplicity, unexpectedness and stories, for making messages memorable. Useful for teachers, marketers, managers and anyone who needs to communicate clearly.

title: Purple Cow
author: Seth Godin
description: Godin argues that traditional advertising is less effective and that products must be genuinely remarkable to stand out. The book gives examples of companies that built remarkable products and offers ideas for doing the same. A short read for marketers and entrepreneurs.

title: Leaders Eat Last
author: Simon Sinek
description: Sinek explores why some teams build deep trust and cooperation while others do not. Drawing on biology, military examples and business cases, he argues that leaders create safety by putting their people first. Aimed at managers and those interested in organisational culture.

title: Extreme Ownership
author: Jocko Willink
description: Two former US Navy SEAL officers apply lessons from combat leadership in Iraq to business. Each chapter pairs a battlefield account with a principle, such as taking ownership of outcomes, and a business example. Practical reading for team leaders and managers.

title: Never Split the Difference
author: Chris Voss
description: A former FBI hostage negotiator presents negotiation techniques based on tactical empathy, active listening and calibrated questions. Chris Voss illustrates each method with stories from crisis negotiations. Useful for business negotiations and everyday conversations.

title: Getting to Yes
author: Roger Fisher
description: From the Harvard Negotiation Project, this book outlines principled negotiation: separating people from the problem, focusing on interests, generating options and using objective criteria. It is short and practical. A standard introduction to negotiation for students and professionals.

title: No Rules Rules
author: Reed Hastings
description: Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings and business professor Erin Meyer describe the company's culture of freedom and responsibility. They explain practices such as high talent density, candid feedback and minimal rules on expenses and holidays. A look at an unconventional management approach.

title: Fast Food Nation
author: Eric Schlosser
description: An investigation of the American fast food industry, from its origins in post-war California to its effects on agriculture, meatpacking, labour and public health. Schlosser combines reporting with economic and historical context. A widely discussed work of investigative journalism.

title: Into Thin Air
author: Jon Krakauer
description: A journalist's first-hand account of the 1996 Mount Everest disaster, in which several climbers died during a storm. Krakauer describes the commercial guided expeditions, the climb and the decisions made under extreme conditions. A gripping work of narrative non-fiction about risk and responsibility.

title: Moneyball
author: Michael Lewis
description: Lewis follows the Oakland Athletics baseball team as its general manager uses statistical analysis to compete with wealthier clubs. The book shows how overlooked data revealed undervalued players. Of interest to readers in sports, data analysis and management.

title: The Boys in the Boat
author: Daniel James Brown
description: The true story of the University of Washington rowing crew, made up largely of working-class young men, who competed at the 1936 Berlin Olympics. Brown focuses on one rower's difficult upbringing alongside the team's development. An inspiring sports history set against the Great Depression.

title: Bad Blood
author: John Carreyrou
description: A Wall Street Journal reporter recounts the rise and fall of Theranos, a start-up that claimed to run many blood tests from a finger prick. Carreyrou describes the company's culture, the investors and the whistleblowers who helped expose it. A cautionary tale about technology, ethics and corporate governance.

title: Factfulness
author: Hans Rosling
description: A physician and statistician explains why many people hold an overly negative view of global trends in health, wealth and education. Rosling identifies common thinking habits that distort understanding and shows how to check claims against data. Useful for students and anyone who works with statistics.

title: Nickel and Dimed
author: Barbara Ehrenreich
description: Ehrenreich takes a series of low-wage jobs in the United States, including waitressing, cleaning and retail work, to see whether she can live on the pay. She describes the physical demands, costs of housing and daily pressures workers face. A well-known piece of immersive reporting on poverty and work.

title: Between the World and Me
author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
description: Written as a letter to his teenage son, this book reflects on what it means to be Black in the United States. Coates draws on his own childhood, education and history to discuss race, violence and vulnerability. A short, personal work of social commentary.

title: Killers of the Flower Moon
author: David Grann
description: Grann investigates a series of murders of members of the Osage Nation in Oklahoma in the 1920s, after oil was found on their land. The book also covers the early FBI's role in the investigation. A detailed work of historical true crime.

title: The Lost City of Z
author: David Grann
description: Grann retraces the expedition of British explorer Percy Fawcett, who disappeared in the Amazon in 1925 while searching for a lost civilisation. The book alternates between Fawcett's story and the author's own journey into the rainforest. Adventure history mixed with modern archaeology.

title: Say Nothing
author: Patrick Radden Keefe
description: Using the 1972 disappearance of a mother of ten in Belfast as its starting point, this book examines the Troubles in Northern Ireland. Keefe follows several people involved in the conflict and its long aftermath. A carefully researched account of political violence and memory.

title: Hiroshima
author: John Hersey
description: John Hersey's report on the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, told through the experiences of six survivors. Originally published in 1946, later editions add what happened to them in the following decades. A landmark of journalism and an important historical record.

title: On Writing
author: Stephen King
description: Stephen King combines a memoir of his development as a writer with practical advice on the craft. He discusses vocabulary, grammar, style, revision and the habits of a working writer. Helpful for aspiring writers and readers interested in how fiction is made.

title: A Room of One's Own
author: Virginia Woolf
description: Based on lectures Virginia Woolf gave at women's colleges in 1928, this essay argues that women need financial independence and private space to write. It examines the history of women and fiction. A foundational text in feminist literary criticism.

title: The Fire Next Time
author: James Baldwin
description: Two essays by James Baldwin on race, religion and American society, written as a letter to his nephew and a reflection on his own experiences. Published in 1963, it was influential during the civil rights movement. A short, powerful work for readers interested in history and social justice.

title: The Histories
author: Herodotus
description: Written in the fifth century BC, Herodotus's account of the wars between the Greeks and the Persian Empire is often called the first work of history. Alongside the conflict, it describes the customs, geography and stories of many ancient peoples. Essential reading for students of the ancient world.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War
author: Thucydides
description: Thucydides' account of the long war between Athens and Sparta in the fifth century BC, written by an Athenian general who lived through it. It includes speeches, battles and analysis of political decisions. A foundational text in history and international relations.

title: Postwar
author: Tony Judt
description: A comprehensive history of Europe from the end of the Second World War in 1945 to the early twenty-first century. Judt covers both Western and Eastern Europe, including reconstruction, the Cold War, the fall of communism and European integration. A detailed reference for students of modern history.

title: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
author: Richard Rhodes
description: Rhodes traces the science and history behind the first nuclear weapons, from early discoveries in atomic physics to the Manhattan Project and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The book profiles the scientists involved and the moral questions they faced. A major work of history of science.

title: Band of Brothers
author: Stephen E. Ambrose
description: Ambrose follows Easy Company of the US Army's 101st Airborne Division from training in 1942 through the Normandy landings and the end of the war in Europe. Based on interviews with veterans, it focuses on the soldiers' experiences. A well-known account of the Second World War.

title: The Origins of Totalitarianism
author: Hannah Arendt
description: Hannah Arendt examines the historical roots of Nazism and Stalinism, tracing antisemitism and imperialism in the nineteenth century before analysing totalitarian movements and regimes. A demanding but influential work of political theory and history. Suited to advanced students of politics and philosophy.

title: India After Gandhi
author: Ramachandra Guha
description: Guha's history of the Republic of India from independence in 1947 onwards. It covers the drafting of the Constitution, the integration of states, wars, political movements, economic change and the challenges of a diverse democracy. A key text for understanding modern India.

title: The Discovery of India
author: Jawaharlal Nehru
description: Written by Jawaharlal Nehru while imprisoned in 1942 to 1946, this book surveys Indian history, philosophy and culture from ancient times to the colonial period. It reflects his thinking about Indian identity and nationhood. An important text in Indian historical and political writing.

title: Freedom at Midnight
author: Larry Collins
description: Collins and Lapierre recount the events surrounding Indian independence and partition in 1947, from the final months of British rule to the violence that followed. The book draws on interviews with many of the people involved. A vivid narrative history for general readers.

title: The Anarchy
author: William Dalrymple
description: Dalrymple tells how the East India Company, a private trading business, came to control much of the Indian subcontinent in the eighteenth century. He describes the decline of the Mughal Empire, wars and the Company's growing power. A detailed history of early colonial India.

title: Stalingrad
author: Antony Beevor
description: Beevor's history of the Battle of Stalingrad from 1942 to 1943, one of the turning points of the Second World War. Using archival sources and soldiers' letters, he covers both the strategy and the experiences of soldiers and civilians. A respected work of military history.

title: Born a Crime
author: Trevor Noah
description: Trevor Noah's memoir of growing up in South Africa during and after apartheid, as the child of a Black mother and a white father at a time when such relationships were illegal. The book combines humour with serious reflection on race, poverty and family. Popular with both young adults and adults.

title: Shoe Dog
author: Phil Knight
description: The memoir of Phil Knight, who started Nike as a small business importing running shoes from Japan. He describes the company's early financial struggles, partnerships and growth. An engaging story of entrepreneurship and persistence.

title: Wings of Fire
author: A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
description: The autobiography of A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, describing his childhood in Rameswaram, his education and his work on India's space and missile programmes. It reflects on hard work, mentorship and service to the nation. Inspiring reading, especially for students in India.

title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!
author: Richard P. Feynman
description: A collection of stories from the life of physicist Richard Feynman, as told to a friend. It covers his curiosity, pranks, work on the Manhattan Project and adventures outside science. An entertaining look at a famous scientist's way of thinking.

title: Benjamin Franklin: An American Life
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Walter Isaacson's biography of Benjamin Franklin, covering his work as a printer, writer, scientist, inventor, diplomat and founding father of the United States. The book places his achievements in historical context. A readable biography for general readers and history students.

title: Alan Turing: The Enigma
author: Andrew Hodges
description: The definitive biography of Alan Turing, the mathematician who laid foundations for computer science and helped break German codes during the Second World War. Hodges covers his work, his persecution for homosexuality and his death. Important reading for computer science and history students.

title: A Beautiful Mind
author: Sylvia Nasar
description: The biography of John Nash, the mathematician whose work in game theory earned a Nobel Prize in economics. Nasar describes his early brilliance, his long struggle with schizophrenia and his recovery. A portrait of genius and mental illness.

title: Night
author: Elie Wiesel
description: Elie Wiesel's memoir of his experiences as a teenager in the Nazi concentration camps of Auschwitz and Buchenwald with his father. It is a short, direct account of the Holocaust and its effect on faith and humanity. Widely read in schools and universities.

title: Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr.
author: Ron Chernow
description: Chernow's biography of John D. Rockefeller, founder of Standard Oil and one of the richest people in history. It covers his business methods, the creation of a monopoly, public criticism and his later philanthropy. A detailed study of American industry and wealth.

title: Grant
author: Ron Chernow
description: Ron Chernow's biography of Ulysses S. Grant, covering his early struggles, his leadership of Union armies in the American Civil War and his presidency. It reassesses his record on Reconstruction and civil rights. A long, detailed biography for history readers.

title: Napoleon: A Life
author: Andrew Roberts
description: Andrew Roberts uses Napoleon's letters to present a comprehensive biography of the French emperor, from his Corsican childhood to his military campaigns, reforms and final exile. The book assesses both his achievements and his failures. Suited to readers interested in European history.

title: Churchill: Walking with Destiny
author: Andrew Roberts
description: Andrew Roberts draws on newly available sources to write a single-volume life of Winston Churchill, from his youth through his wartime leadership to old age. He examines both his successes and his mistakes. A comprehensive biography of a major twentieth-century figure.

title: A Promised Land
author: Barack Obama
description: The first volume of Barack Obama's presidential memoirs, covering his early political career, the 2008 election and much of his first term. He discusses major decisions on the economy, healthcare and foreign policy. Of interest to readers of politics and recent history.

title: Dreams from My Father
author: Barack Obama
description: Barack Obama's memoir, written before his political career, about his childhood in Hawaii and Indonesia, his search for identity and his visit to his father's family in Kenya. It reflects on race, family and belonging. A personal account of identity and heritage.

title: Kitchen Confidential
author: Anthony Bourdain
description: Chef Anthony Bourdain describes life behind the scenes in restaurant kitchens, from his early jobs to running a New York brasserie. He writes candidly about the culture, pressures and personalities of the trade. A lively memoir for readers interested in food and work.

title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin
description: Charles Darwin's 1859 work presenting the theory of evolution by natural selection, supported by observations from nature, breeding and fossils. It reshaped biology and our understanding of life. A foundational scientific text for students of biology.

title: What If?
author: Randall Munroe
description: Randall Munroe, creator of the xkcd webcomic, answers unusual hypothetical questions using physics, mathematics and cartoons. Each answer works through the science step by step with humour. An entertaining introduction to scientific reasoning for curious readers.

title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
author: Thomas S. Kuhn
description: Kuhn argues that science progresses through periods of normal research punctuated by revolutions in which one paradigm replaces another. The book introduced the idea of the paradigm shift. A key work in the history and philosophy of science.

title: The Demon-Haunted World
author: Carl Sagan
description: Carl Sagan explains the scientific method and why critical thinking matters, using examples of pseudoscience, superstition and hoaxes. He offers a toolkit for evaluating claims. Valuable reading for students and anyone interested in reasoning and evidence.

title: Pale Blue Dot
author: Carl Sagan
description: Sagan reflects on humanity's place in the universe, inspired by the photograph of Earth taken by Voyager 1 from billions of kilometres away. The book surveys planetary exploration and considers the future of human space travel. A thoughtful work of popular astronomy.

title: The Blind Watchmaker
author: Richard Dawkins
description: Dawkins explains how natural selection can produce complex living things without a designer. He uses examples and computer simulations to show cumulative selection at work. A popular science classic on evolution.

title: The Code Breaker
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Isaacson's account of Jennifer Doudna and the development of CRISPR gene editing. The book explains the science, the competition among researchers and the ethical questions raised by editing human genes. Of interest to students of biology and general readers.

title: Brief Answers to the Big Questions
author: Stephen Hawking
description: Stephen Hawking's final book addresses questions such as how the universe began, whether there is other intelligent life, and whether we can predict the future. Short chapters present his views in accessible language. A good introduction to his thinking.

title: The Universe in a Nutshell
author: Stephen Hawking
description: Hawking explains ideas in modern physics, including relativity, quantum theory, the shape of time, black holes and the possibility of time travel. The book is heavily illustrated to help non-specialists. A companion to his earlier popular science writing.

title: Entangled Life
author: Merlin Sheldrake
description: A biologist explores the world of fungi, from networks that connect plant roots to yeasts, moulds and mushrooms. Sheldrake explains how fungi shape ecosystems, medicine and human culture. An engaging work of popular biology.

title: The Body: A Guide for Occupants
author: Bill Bryson
description: Bill Bryson tours the human body, explaining how its organs and systems work, how diseases affect it and how medicine has developed. The book is full of facts and stories. Accessible reading for general audiences and students.

title: Lab Girl
author: Hope Jahren
description: Geobotanist Hope Jahren combines memoir with writing about trees, seeds and soil. She describes building research laboratories and her partnership with a long-time colleague. A personal view of scientific life for students and general readers.

title: Your Inner Fish
author: Neil Shubin
description: A palaeontologist who helped discover the fossil Tiktaalik explains how the human body reflects our evolutionary history. Shubin traces features such as hands, teeth and ears back to ancient ancestors. An accessible introduction to evolution and anatomy.

title: The Disappearing Spoon
author: Sam Kean
publisher: Little, Brown Books for Young Readers
description: Kean tells stories behind the elements of the periodic table, covering their discovery, uses and the people involved. The book links chemistry to history, war, medicine and everyday life. An entertaining companion to chemistry studies.

title: The Second Machine Age
author: Erik Brynjolfsson
description: Two MIT researchers examine how digital technologies such as robotics, artificial intelligence and networks are transforming work and the economy. They discuss rising productivity alongside growing inequality and suggest policies in response. Useful for students of economics, business and technology.

title: The Inevitable
author: Kevin Kelly
description: Kevin Kelly identifies twelve long-term technological trends, such as sharing, tracking, remixing and filtering, that he expects to shape the coming decades. Each chapter explains a trend and its likely effects on everyday life. A forward-looking read on digital culture.

title: Weapons of Math Destruction
author: Cathy O'Neil
description: A data scientist shows how algorithms used in hiring, lending, policing, insurance and education can reinforce bias and inequality. O'Neil explains why opaque, large-scale models can harm people without accountability. Important reading for anyone studying data science or technology ethics.

title: The Shallows
author: Nicholas Carr
description: Carr examines how internet use may be changing the way people read, think and remember. He draws on neuroscience and the history of media to argue that constant online distraction encourages shallower thinking. A thought-provoking read for students and educators.

title: Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution
author: Steven Levy
description: Steven Levy chronicles the programmers and engineers who shaped early computing culture, from MIT in the 1950s to the personal computer pioneers and game developers of the 1980s. The book describes the hacker ethic of sharing and curiosity. A classic history of computing culture.

title: Kubernetes: Up and Running
author: Kelsey Hightower
description: An introduction to Kubernetes, the open-source system for deploying and managing containerised applications. Written by early contributors to the project, it covers pods, services, deployments, storage and operating clusters. Practical for developers and operations engineers.

title: The Unicorn Project
author: Gene Kim
description: A novel set in the same fictional company as The Phoenix Project, told from the perspective of a developer trying to improve how software is built. It illustrates ideas about developer productivity, flow and modern DevOps. An accessible way to learn about software delivery practices.

title: Team Topologies
author: Matthew Skelton
description: Skelton and Pais present a model for organising software teams around four team types and three interaction modes. The book links team structure to software architecture and fast delivery. Useful for engineering managers and architects.

title: Release It!
author: Michael T. Nygard
description: A guide to designing and deploying software that survives real-world production conditions. Nygard describes stability patterns such as timeouts and circuit breakers, along with common failure modes and operational practices. Valuable for developers building online systems.

title: Building Microservices
author: Sam Newman
description: Sam Newman explains how to design, build and run systems made of small, independently deployable services. Topics include modelling services, integration, testing, deployment, monitoring, security and organisational impact. A standard reference for software architects.

title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
author: Shoshana Zuboff
description: Zuboff argues that major technology companies have created a new economic model based on collecting and analysing personal data to predict and influence behaviour. She examines the social and political consequences. A substantial work on privacy and the digital economy.

title: Chip War
author: Chris Miller
description: A history of the semiconductor industry from its origins in the United States to today's global supply chain. Miller explains how control of chip design and manufacturing became central to economic and military power. Relevant to readers interested in technology, geopolitics and business.

title: The Soul of a New Machine
author: Tracy Kidder
description: Tracy Kidder follows a team of engineers at Data General as they race to design a new minicomputer in the late 1970s. The book captures the pressure, creativity and teamwork of hardware and software development. A Pulitzer Prize-winning classic about engineering work.

title: Where Wizards Stay Up Late
author: Katie Hafner
description: Hafner and Lyon tell the story of the creation of ARPANET, the network that became the foundation of the internet. The book profiles the researchers and engineers involved and explains the key technical ideas. A readable history of networking.

title: Don't Make Me Think
author: Steve Krug
description: Steve Krug's guide to web and mobile usability, explaining how people actually use websites and how to design clear, simple interfaces. It includes advice on navigation, page layout and running inexpensive usability tests. Short and practical for designers and developers.

title: Pro Git
author: Scott Chacon
description: A comprehensive guide to the Git version control system, covering basic commands, branching, remote repositories, collaboration workflows and Git's internals. Written by members of the Git community. Useful for beginners and experienced developers alike.

title: Mastering Bitcoin
author: Andreas M. Antonopoulos
description: A technical guide to how Bitcoin works, covering keys and addresses, wallets, transactions, the blockchain, mining and the peer-to-peer network. It includes code examples for developers. Suitable for programmers and students who want to understand cryptocurrency in depth.

title: Rework
author: Jason Fried
description: The founders of the software company 37signals offer short essays challenging conventional business advice. They argue for staying small, avoiding unnecessary meetings and planning, and launching early. A quick, opinionated read for founders and small teams.

title: Founders at Work
author: Jessica Livingston
description: Jessica Livingston interviews founders of well-known technology companies about their early days, including how they found ideas, raised money and survived setbacks. The interviews show how messy and uncertain starting a company can be. Valuable reading for aspiring entrepreneurs.

title: Traction
author: Gabriel Weinberg
description: Weinberg and Mares describe nineteen channels a start-up can use to gain customers, including search engine marketing, content, partnerships and sales. They present a framework for testing channels and focusing on the most promising ones. A practical guide for early-stage founders.

title: Running Lean
author: Ash Maurya
description: Ash Maurya presents a systematic method for testing a business idea before investing heavily in it. The book introduces the Lean Canvas and explains how to identify risky assumptions, interview customers and measure progress. A hands-on guide for founders and product teams.

title: Disciplined Entrepreneurship
author: Bill Aulet
description: A step-by-step framework from MIT for building a new venture, covering market segmentation, customer profiling, value proposition, business model and product planning. Each step includes worked examples. Suited to students and first-time founders.

title: The Four Steps to the Epiphany
author: Steven Gary Blank
description: Steve Blank introduces customer development, a process for discovering and validating customers alongside product development. The book outlines four stages from customer discovery to company building. A foundational text behind the lean start-up approach.

title: Inspired: How to Create Tech Products Customers Love
author: Marty Cagan
description: Marty Cagan explains how leading technology companies discover and build successful products. He covers the role of product managers, empowered teams, product discovery techniques and company culture. A standard reference for product managers and founders.

title: Lean Analytics
author: Alistair Croll
description: Croll and Yoskovitz explain how start-ups can use data to measure progress and make decisions. They introduce the idea of focusing on one metric that matters at each stage and give benchmarks for different business models. Practical for founders and growth teams.

title: The Art of the Start
author: Guy Kawasaki
description: Guy Kawasaki offers practical advice for launching a new venture, including positioning, pitching, writing a business plan, recruiting, raising money and building a brand. The tone is direct and lively. Suitable for entrepreneurs in start-ups and non-profits.

title: Value Proposition Design
author: Alexander Osterwalder
description: A companion to Business Model Generation that focuses on understanding customers and designing products they want. It introduces the Value Proposition Canvas and practical tools for testing ideas. Useful for founders, product managers and students.

title: That Will Never Work
author: Marc Randolph
description: Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph recounts how the company began as a DVD-by-mail service and survived its early years. He shares lessons on testing ideas, building a team and handling doubt. An engaging start-up story with practical takeaways.

title: Delivering Happiness
author: Tony Hsieh
description: Tony Hsieh describes his path from early ventures to leading the online retailer Zappos, focusing on customer service and company culture. He explains how the company built its values. A business memoir for readers interested in culture-driven companies.

title: The Founder's Dilemmas
author: Noam Wasserman
description: A Harvard professor uses data from thousands of start-ups to examine early decisions founders face, such as whether to found alone or with others, how to split equity and when to hire or raise money. He shows the trade-offs behind each choice. A research-based guide for founders.

title: Startup Communities
author: Brad Feld
description: Brad Feld explains how to build a thriving entrepreneurial ecosystem in any city, drawing on his experience in Boulder, Colorado. He argues that entrepreneurs must lead the effort, supported by universities, investors and government. Relevant for founders and community organisers.

title: Built to Sell
author: John Warrillow
description: Through a story about an agency owner, Warrillow explains how to create a business that can run without its founder and be sold. Key ideas include standardising a product, reducing dependence on the owner and creating predictable revenue. Practical for small business owners.

title: Losing My Virginity
author: Richard Branson
description: Richard Branson's autobiography covers his early ventures, the founding of Virgin Records and Virgin Atlantic, and his many business adventures. He describes risks, failures and successes in an informal style. An entertaining story of entrepreneurship.

title: How I Built This
author: Guy Raz
description: Based on the podcast of the same name, Guy Raz draws lessons from interviews with founders of well-known companies. Chapters follow the stages of building a business, from finding an idea to growth and setbacks. Accessible and encouraging for new entrepreneurs.

title: Trillion Dollar Coach
author: Eric Schmidt
description: Former Google leaders describe the coaching approach of Bill Campbell, a mentor to executives at Google, Apple and other companies. They explain his principles on trust, teamwork and caring for people. Useful for managers and founders.

title: Secrets of Sand Hill Road
author: Scott Kupor
description: A venture capitalist explains how venture capital firms raise funds, choose investments and structure deals. Kupor covers term sheets, board dynamics and exits from the founder's perspective. Valuable for entrepreneurs seeking investment.

title: Hatching Twitter
author: Nick Bilton
description: A journalist tells the story of Twitter's founding and early years, focusing on the founders and their conflicts over control of the company. The book shows how personal relationships shaped a major technology firm. A narrative case study of start-up power struggles.

title: Drive
author: Daniel H. Pink
description: Daniel Pink argues that people are motivated more by autonomy, mastery and purpose than by rewards and punishments for many kinds of work. He draws on research in psychology and economics. Useful for students, teachers, managers and parents.

title: Ego Is the Enemy
author: Ryan Holiday
publisher: Portfolio / Penguin, an imprint ofPenguin Random House LLC
description: Ryan Holiday draws on historical figures and Stoic philosophy to show how ego can block learning, success and recovery from failure. The book is divided into stages of aspiration, success and failure. A reflective read on humility and self-awareness.

title: Unlimited Power
author: Tony Robbins
description: Tony Robbins presents techniques for personal achievement based on neuro-linguistic programming, including managing emotional states, setting goals and modelling successful people. An influential book in the personal development genre.

title: The Compound Effect
author: Darren Hardy
description: Darren Hardy explains how small, consistent choices and habits add up to large results over time. He offers practical steps for tracking behaviour, building momentum and staying on course. A straightforward guide to steady self-improvement.

title: The Slight Edge
author: Jeff Olson
description: Jeff Olson argues that success or failure comes from simple daily actions that seem insignificant in the moment. He explains how to choose small positive habits and keep them up over time. An encouraging read on consistency and long-term thinking.

title: Relentless
author: Tim S. Grover
description: Tim Grover, a trainer of elite athletes including Michael Jordan, describes the mindset he believes separates great performers from good ones. The book focuses on drive, discipline and handling pressure. Direct reading for athletes and competitive people.

title: Outwitting the Devil
author: Napoleon Hill
description: Written in 1938 but published decades later, this book by Napoleon Hill presents an imagined conversation about fear, procrastination and habits that hold people back. Annotated editions add modern commentary. A classic of motivational literature.

title: The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari
author: Robin Sharma
description: A fable about a successful lawyer who suffers a health crisis, travels to India and returns with lessons from a group of sages. Robin Sharma uses the story to present ideas on purpose, discipline and inner peace. A popular, easy-to-read motivational book.

title: The Last Lecture
author: Randy Pausch
description: Computer science professor Randy Pausch expands on his final lecture, given after learning he had terminal cancer. He reflects on childhood dreams, enabling the dreams of others and living well. A moving and widely read book.

title: Tuesdays with Morrie
author: Mitch Albom
description: Sportswriter Mitch Albom recounts weekly visits to his former college professor Morrie Schwartz during the last months of Morrie's life. Their conversations cover love, work, ageing, regret and death. A short, reflective memoir.

title: You Can Win
author: Shiv Khera
description: Shiv Khera offers practical advice on building a positive attitude, self-esteem, good habits and goal setting. Each chapter includes examples and action points. Popular with students and professionals in India and elsewhere.

title: The 10X Rule
author: Grant Cardone
description: Grant Cardone argues that most people underestimate the effort needed to reach their goals and should set targets and take action at ten times their usual level. The book focuses on ambition, persistence and sales. A high-energy read for driven readers.

title: Mastery
author: Robert Greene
description: Robert Greene studies the lives of historical and contemporary masters to describe the path to excellence in a field. He covers finding one's calling, apprenticeship, mentorship and creative work. A long, detailed guide for anyone pursuing a serious craft.

title: So Good They Can't Ignore You
author: Cal Newport
description: Cal Newport challenges the advice to follow your passion, arguing that valuable skills and career capital matter more for finding satisfying work. He shares examples and practical strategies. Helpful for students choosing careers and early-career professionals.

title: Steal Like an Artist
author: Austin Kleon
description: A short, illustrated guide to creativity by Austin Kleon. He encourages readers to learn from others' work, collect influences and develop their own voice through practice. Accessible inspiration for students, writers and artists.

title: Big Magic
author: Elizabeth Gilbert
description: Elizabeth Gilbert shares her views on creativity, fear and inspiration, encouraging readers to pursue creative work for its own sake. The book mixes personal stories with practical encouragement. Aimed at anyone wanting to live a more creative life.

title: The 5 Second Rule
author: Mel Robbins
description: Mel Robbins describes a simple technique of counting down from five to push oneself into action before hesitation takes over. She applies it to procrastination, confidence and anxiety. A quick, practical read.

title: Discipline Equals Freedom
author: Jocko Willink
description: A short field manual by former Navy SEAL officer Jocko Willink on building self-discipline. It covers mindset, sleep, nutrition and physical training, with workout plans. Direct and practical for readers seeking structure.

title: Limitless
author: Jim Kwik
description: Jim Kwik presents methods for improving learning, focus and memory, organised around mindset, motivation and methods. The book includes exercises for reading faster and remembering more. Aimed at students and lifelong learners.

title: Greenlights
author: Matthew McConaughey
description: Actor Matthew McConaughey shares stories, journal entries and reflections from his life and career. He presents his philosophy of approaching challenges as opportunities. An informal memoir with motivational themes.

title: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat
author: Oliver Sacks
description: Neurologist Oliver Sacks describes cases of patients with unusual neurological conditions affecting perception, memory and identity. Each case is told with compassion and curiosity. A classic introduction to how the brain shapes experience.

title: Nudge
author: Richard H. Thaler
description: An economist and a legal scholar explain how the way choices are presented, or choice architecture, influences decisions about health, money and happiness. They argue for designing choices that help people while preserving freedom. Influential in behavioural economics and public policy.

title: Misbehaving
author: Richard H. Thaler
description: Richard Thaler tells the story of how behavioural economics developed, as he and others challenged the assumption that people always act rationally. He explains key ideas such as mental accounting and the endowment effect. An accessible history of the field.

title: Behave
author: Robert M. Sapolsky
description: A neuroscientist and primatologist explains human behaviour by working backwards in time, from the brain activity a second before an action to hormones, childhood, culture and evolution. Sapolsky covers violence, cooperation and morality. A wide-ranging, detailed book.

title: Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers
author: Robert M. Sapolsky
description: Sapolsky explains the biology of stress, why animals recover quickly while humans often suffer from chronic stress, and how stress affects health. Topics include sleep, memory, ageing and depression. Accessible for students of psychology and biology.

title: Games People Play
author: Eric Berne
description: Eric Berne describes the repeated patterns of interaction, or games, that people use in relationships, based on his theory of transactional analysis. He catalogues common games and their hidden motives. A classic of popular psychology.

title: Attached
author: Amir Levine
description: A psychiatrist and a psychologist explain adult attachment theory and the three main attachment styles: anxious, avoidant and secure. They show how these styles affect romantic relationships. Practical reading for anyone interested in relationships.

title: The Social Animal
author: Elliot Aronson
description: A widely used introduction to social psychology, covering conformity, persuasion, prejudice, aggression, attraction and self-justification. Aronson explains classic experiments and their implications. Suitable for introductory psychology students.

title: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
author: Carol Tavris
description: Two social psychologists explain cognitive dissonance and how it leads people to justify bad decisions rather than admit mistakes. Examples come from politics, law, medicine and personal relationships. An engaging introduction to self-justification.

title: The Undoing Project
author: Michael Lewis
description: Michael Lewis tells the story of the partnership between psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, whose research on judgement and decision-making founded behavioural economics. The book covers their ideas and their friendship. Readable history of science.

title: Lost Connections
author: Johann Hari
description: Johann Hari investigates causes of depression and anxiety beyond brain chemistry, including disconnection from meaningful work, other people and values. He discusses research and possible ways to reconnect. A personal and journalistic exploration of mental health.

title: Feeling Good
author: David D. Burns
description: A psychiatrist presents cognitive behavioural techniques for overcoming depression, such as identifying and challenging distorted thoughts. The book includes exercises and self-assessment tools. A long-standing self-help guide grounded in clinical research.

title: The Psychopath Test
author: Jon Ronson
description: Journalist Jon Ronson investigates psychopathy and the checklist used to diagnose it, meeting psychologists, patients and executives along the way. He questions how mental illness is labelled. An entertaining look at psychiatry and its limits.

title: SQL Antipatterns
author: Bill Karwin
description: Bill Karwin describes common mistakes in database design and SQL queries, such as storing lists in a single column, and explains why they cause problems. Each antipattern comes with better solutions. Practical for developers working with relational databases.

title: Learning SQL
author: Alan Beaulieu
description: A beginner's guide to SQL covering queries, filtering, joins, grouping, subqueries, transactions, indexes and views. Examples use a sample database. Suitable for students and developers new to relational databases.

title: Sams Teach Yourself SQL in 10 Minutes
author: Ben Forta
description: A compact introduction to SQL organised into short lessons, each designed to be completed quickly. It covers retrieving, sorting, filtering, joining and modifying data across common database systems. Handy as a quick reference.

title: Fundamentals of Database Systems
author: Ramez Elmasri
description: A comprehensive textbook covering data modelling, the relational model, SQL, normalisation, storage and indexing, query processing, transactions, concurrency and recovery. It also introduces NoSQL and big data topics. Widely used in university database courses.

title: Database Management Systems
author: Raghu Ramakrishnan
description: A textbook on the design and implementation of database systems, covering relational algebra, SQL, storage, indexing, query evaluation and optimisation, transactions and database design. It balances theory with system internals. Used in undergraduate and graduate courses.

title: An Introduction to Database Systems
author: C. J. Date
description: C. J. Date's long-standing textbook on database theory and practice, with a strong focus on the relational model. It covers relational algebra and calculus, normalisation, integrity, views, recovery and concurrency. A classic reference for database students.

title: Joe Celko's SQL for Smarties
author: Joe Celko
description: A collection of advanced SQL techniques for solving difficult problems, such as handling hierarchies, temporal data and complex aggregations. Celko emphasises thinking in sets. Suitable for experienced SQL programmers.

title: Database Internals
author: Alex Petrov
description: Alex Petrov explains how database storage engines and distributed databases work under the hood. Topics include B-trees, log-structured storage, transaction processing, replication and consensus algorithms. Useful for engineers who build or operate data systems.

title: MongoDB in Action
author: Kyle Banker
description: A practical guide to MongoDB covering document modelling, queries, indexing, aggregation, replication and sharding. Examples show how to build applications on the database. Suited to developers new to document databases.

title: Refactoring Databases
author: Scott W. Ambler
description: Ambler and Sadalage describe techniques for evolving a database schema safely through small, tested changes. The book catalogues refactorings for structure, data quality and referential integrity. Useful for teams practising agile development.

title: Graph Databases
author: Ian Robinson
description: An introduction to graph databases, explaining how to model data as nodes and relationships and query it efficiently. Examples use Neo4j and the Cypher query language. Suitable for developers exploring connected data.

title: Learning MySQL
author: Seyed M. M. Tahaghoghi
description: A practical guide to MySQL covering installation, SQL queries, database design, user management, backups and performance basics. Suitable for beginners who want to use MySQL in applications.

title: The Art of SQL
author: Stéphane Faroult
description: Stéphane Faroult explains how to write efficient SQL by thinking about how queries interact with database structures. Chapters use military strategy as a theme to discuss design, indexing and query patterns. For developers who want faster, more scalable queries.

title: Transaction Processing
author: Jim Gray
description: A detailed technical reference on transaction processing systems by Jim Gray and Andreas Reuter. It covers concurrency control, recovery, logging, locking and system architecture. A foundational text for engineers building reliable databases.

title: Database Reliability Engineering
author: Laine Campbell
description: Campbell and Majors apply site reliability engineering ideas to databases, covering service levels, risk management, infrastructure, backup and recovery, security and operational practices. Useful for engineers responsible for production databases.

title: Practical SQL
author: Anthony DeBarros
description: A beginner-friendly introduction to SQL using PostgreSQL and real public datasets. It covers queries, joins, statistics, text and geographic data. Suitable for data journalists, analysts and students.

title: Elasticsearch: The Definitive Guide
author: Clinton Gormley
description: A guide to Elasticsearch, the open-source search and analytics engine. It covers indexing, searching, relevance scoring, aggregations and running clusters. Useful for developers adding search to applications.

title: T-SQL Fundamentals
author: Itzik Ben-Gan
description: An introduction to querying Microsoft SQL Server with Transact-SQL. It covers single-table queries, joins, subqueries, set operators, window functions, data modification and transactions, with an emphasis on set-based thinking. Suitable for beginners.

title: Head First SQL
author: Lynn Beighley
description: A visual, conversational introduction to SQL and database design, covering creating tables, writing queries, joins, normalisation and security basics. Puzzles and exercises reinforce learning. Aimed at beginners.

title: Unix Network Programming
author: W. Richard Stevens
description: The classic guide to writing networked programs using the sockets API on Unix-like systems. It covers TCP and UDP, I/O models, name resolution, broadcasting, multicasting and threads, with extensive code. Essential for systems and network programmers.

title: Internetworking with TCP/IP
author: Douglas E. Comer
description: Douglas Comer's textbook on the principles, protocols and architecture of the TCP/IP internet. It explains addressing, routing, IP, TCP, UDP and higher-level services. Used in university networking courses.

title: Interconnections
author: Radia Perlman
description: Radia Perlman, inventor of the spanning tree protocol, explains how bridges, switches and routers work and the trade-offs in their design. She covers addressing, routing algorithms and network protocols. A respected reference for network engineers.

title: Data Communications and Networking
author: Behrouz A. Forouzan
description: Forouzan's textbook introduces data communications and networking using a layered approach, from the physical layer to the application layer. It includes many figures, examples and exercises. Popular in undergraduate courses, especially in India.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Suite
author: Behrouz A. Forouzan
description: Forouzan explains the TCP/IP protocols layer by layer, including IP addressing, routing, ARP, ICMP, UDP, TCP, DNS and application protocols. Clear diagrams support each topic. Designed for students taking networking courses.

title: Routing TCP/IP
author: Jeff Doyle
description: A detailed guide to interior routing protocols, including RIP, EIGRP, OSPF and IS-IS, with configuration examples on Cisco routers. It explains how routing protocols work and how to troubleshoot them. Useful for network engineers and certification candidates.

title: Network Programmability and Automation
author: Jason Edelman
description: A practical introduction to automating network operations using Linux, Python, data formats, templates, APIs and tools like Ansible and Git. Written for network engineers moving towards software-driven networking.

title: High Performance Browser Networking
author: Ilya Grigorik
description: Ilya Grigorik explains the networking factors that affect web performance, including latency, TCP, TLS, wireless networks, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, WebSocket and WebRTC. He offers practical optimisation advice. Valuable for web developers and engineers.

title: HTTP: The Definitive Guide
author: David Gourley
description: A comprehensive reference to the HTTP protocol, covering messages, connections, proxies, caching, gateways, security and content negotiation. It explains how web clients and servers communicate. Useful for web developers and systems engineers.

title: BGP
author: Iljitsch van Beijnum
description: An introduction to the Border Gateway Protocol, which routes traffic between networks on the internet. The book covers BGP operation, configuration, routing policy, multihoming and traffic engineering. Practical for network administrators.

title: Networking All-in-One For Dummies
author: Doug Lowe
description: A broad reference covering how to plan, set up and manage computer networks, including hardware, Windows and Linux servers, wireless networks, security and cloud services. Written in an approachable style for beginners and small-office administrators.

title: CompTIA Network+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide
author: Mike Meyers
description: A study guide for the CompTIA Network+ certification, covering network models, cabling, TCP/IP, routing, switching, wireless, security and troubleshooting. Includes practice questions. Suitable for exam candidates and networking beginners.

title: Top-Down Network Design
author: Priscilla Oppenheimer
description: A methodology for designing enterprise networks by starting from business goals and working down to logical and physical design. It covers requirements analysis, addressing, routing, security and testing. Used in network design courses.

title: Understanding Linux Network Internals
author: Christian Benvenuti
description: A detailed look at how the Linux kernel implements networking, including device drivers, bridging, IPv4, neighbour discovery and routing. Intended for kernel developers and advanced engineers.

title: Linux Network Administrator's Guide
author: Tony Bautts
description: A practical guide to configuring networking on Linux systems, covering TCP/IP setup, name services, firewalls, email, NFS and other common services. Useful for system administrators.

title: IPv6 Essentials
author: Silvia Hagen
description: An introduction to IPv6, the newer internet protocol, covering addressing, packet structure, ICMPv6, neighbour discovery, security, routing and transition from IPv4. Useful for engineers planning IPv6 deployments.

title: The Illustrated Network
author: Walter Goralski
description: A textbook that explains TCP/IP networking using real packet captures and configurations from a working network. It covers protocols from the link layer to applications, along with routing and security. Useful for students who learn by example.

title: Tubes
author: Andrew Blum
description: A journalist travels to see the physical infrastructure of the internet, including data centres, exchange points and undersea cables. Andrew Blum shows that the network is made of real places and machines. An accessible introduction for general readers.

title: Computer Networks and Internets
author: Douglas E. Comer
description: Douglas Comer's introductory textbook on networking, covering data communications, packet switching, local and wide area networks, internetworking and network applications. Written for students taking a first networking course.

title: 802.11 Wireless Networks: The Definitive Guide
author: Matthew S. Gast
description: A technical guide to Wi-Fi networks based on the IEEE 802.11 standards. It explains the physical and MAC layers, security, deployment and analysis of wireless networks. Useful for engineers and administrators.

title: The Code Book
author: Simon Singh
description: Simon Singh tells the history of codes and ciphers from ancient times to modern public-key cryptography. The book explains how codes were made and broken, including the Enigma machine. Accessible for general readers and students.

title: Applied Cryptography
author: Bruce Schneier
description: Bruce Schneier's comprehensive reference to cryptographic protocols, algorithms and source code. It covers symmetric and public-key cryptography, digital signatures, key management and practical protocol design. A classic for security engineers.

title: Cryptography Engineering
author: Niels Ferguson
description: A practical guide to designing and implementing cryptographic systems correctly. The authors cover block ciphers, hash functions, message authentication, key negotiation, randomness and public-key infrastructure. Useful for developers building secure software.

title: Security Engineering
author: Ross Anderson
description: Ross Anderson's broad guide to building systems that remain dependable in the face of error and malice. It covers cryptography, access control, protocols, banking, hardware, psychology and policy. A comprehensive reference for security students and practitioners.

title: Countdown to Zero Day
author: Kim Zetter
description: Kim Zetter investigates Stuxnet, the computer worm designed to sabotage Iran's nuclear programme. The book explains how security researchers discovered and analysed it, and what it meant for cyber warfare. A detailed work of technology journalism.

title: Sandworm
author: Andy Greenberg
description: Andy Greenberg reports on a group of Russian state-backed hackers responsible for attacks on Ukraine's power grid and the NotPetya malware outbreak. He describes the investigators who tracked them. A gripping account of modern cyber warfare.

title: The Cuckoo's Egg
author: Clifford Stoll
description: An astronomer working as a systems administrator traces a small accounting error to a hacker breaking into US military and research computers in the 1980s. Stoll's account shows early network security investigation in action. A classic true story.

title: This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends
author: Nicole Perlroth
description: A New York Times reporter investigates the market for zero-day vulnerabilities and how governments buy and use them for cyber operations. The book traces the rise of cyber weapons and their risks. Important reading on security and policy.

title: Black Hat Python
author: Justin Seitz
description: Justin Seitz shows how to write Python tools for security testing, including network sniffers, web scanners, trojans and forensic scripts. It is aimed at penetration testers and security researchers. Some programming background is assumed.

title: Penetration Testing
author: Georgia Weidman
description: Georgia Weidman provides a hands-on introduction to penetration testing, covering setting up a lab, information gathering, exploitation, password attacks, web and wireless testing, and post-exploitation. Suited to beginners in ethical hacking.

title: The Art of Deception
author: Kevin D. Mitnick
description: Kevin Mitnick, once a well-known hacker, explains how social engineers manipulate people into revealing information or granting access. The book uses scenarios to show common tactics and how organisations can defend against them. Useful for security awareness.

title: The Art of Invisibility
author: Kevin D. Mitnick
description: Mitnick explains how personal data is collected and tracked online and offers practical steps for protecting privacy. Topics include passwords, encryption, browsing, email and mobile devices. Aimed at general readers concerned about privacy.

title: Serious Cryptography
author: Jean-Philippe Aumasson
description: A practical introduction to modern cryptography, explaining how algorithms such as AES, hash functions, RSA and elliptic curves work and how they can fail. It avoids heavy mathematics while staying precise. Suitable for developers and security students.

title: Secrets and Lies
author: Bruce Schneier
description: Bruce Schneier explains why security is a process rather than a product, covering threats, attacks, cryptography, networks and human factors. He argues for thinking about systems as a whole. Accessible to managers and technical readers.

title: Data and Goliath
author: Bruce Schneier
description: Schneier examines mass surveillance by governments and companies, explaining how data is collected and used and why it matters for privacy and freedom. He proposes legal and technical responses. Relevant to students of security, law and policy.

title: Click Here to Kill Everybody
author: Bruce Schneier
